contenido: 1. Therefore, we not only exhorted then to seek the peace of Christ in the kingdom of Christ, but, furthermore, we promised that for this purpose we would do everything possible for us. In the kingdom of Christ, we said: for we were persuaded that there is no more effective means of restoring and invigorating peace than to seek the restoration of the reign of Jesus Christ.

2. Meanwhile, the favorable attitude of the people towards Christ and his Church, the only one that can save them, continued to give us solid hope for better times; a new attitude in some, revived in others, from which it could be deduced that many who until then had been as if exiled from the kingdom of the Redeemer, for having despised his sovereignty, were happily preparing and even hurrying to return to their duties of obedience.

3. Because it is marvelous how much the Missionary Exposition has moved souls, which offered everyone to know well, now the tireless effort of the Church to expand more and more the kingdom of her Spouse throughout all the continents and islands - even, of these, those with the most remote seas - and now the growing number of regions conquered for the Catholic faith by the blood and sweat of the most valiant and undefeated. missionaries, pray also the vast regions that still remain to be subjected to the gentle and saving sovereignty of our King.

4. This reign of our Savior has also seemed to shine like a new light when We Ourselves, after verifying the extraordinary merits and virtues of six virgins and confessors, have elevated them to the honor of the altars, Oh, how much joy and how much consolation filled our soul when, after Us had promulgated the decrees of canonization, an immense crowd of faithful, filled with gratitude, sang the Tu, Rex gloriae Christe in the majestic temple of Saint Peter!

5. Likewise, as the 16th Centenary of the Council of Nicaea falls in the Jubilee Year, it is with even greater pleasure that we command this feast to be celebrated, and we ourselves celebrate it in the Vatican Basilica, since that sacred council defined and proclaimed as a dogma of Catholic faith the consubstantiality of the Only Begotten Son with the Father, in addition to the fact that, by including the words whose kingdom will have no end in its Symbol or formula of faith, it promulgated the royal dignity of Jesus Christ.

6. It has been a very general and ancient custom to call Jesus Christ King, in a metaphorical sense, because of the supreme degree of excellence that he possesses and that exalts him among all created things. Thus, it is said that He reigns in the intelligences of men, not so much because of the sublime and highest degree of His science but because He is the Truth and because men need to drink from Him and obediently receive the truth. It is also said that He reigns in the wills of men, not only because in Him the human will is entirely and perfectly submitted to the holy divine will, but also because with His motions and inspirations He influences our free will and ignites it in very noble purposes. Finally, it is truly said that Christ reigns in the hearts of men because, with his supereminent charity[1] and with his meekness and benignity, he makes himself loved by souls in such a way that no one â€”among all those bornâ€”has ever been or will ever be as loved as Christ Jesus. But, now entering fully into the matter, it is evident that also in the proper and strict sense the title and power of King belongs to Jesus Christ as a man; For only as a man is it said of Him that He received power, honor and the kingdom from the Father[2]; because as the Word of God, whose substance is identical to that of the Father, he cannot help but have in common with him what is proper to divinity and, therefore, also possess as the Father the same supreme and absolute empire over all creatures.
7. That Christ is King, the Holy Scriptures say at every step.

8. To this testimony are added other, even more copious, testimony from the prophets, and mainly the well-known one from Isaiah: A Child has been born to us and a Son has been given to us, who carries the principality on his shoulders; and his name will be the Wonderful One, the Counselor, God, the Mighty One, the Father of the age to come, the Prince of Peace. His empire will be amplified and peace will have no end; He will sit on the seat of David, and will possess his kingdom to strengthen and consolidate it, making equity and justice reign from now on and forever.[7] The same thing that Isaiah predicts the other prophets. Thus Jeremiah, when he predicts that from the line of David the righteous offspring will be born, who like the son of David will reign as King and will be wise and judge on the earth[8]. Thus Daniel, when announcing that the God of heaven will found a kingdom, which will never be destroyed..., will remain eternally[9]; and shortly after he adds: I was observing during the night vision, and behold, a personage who looked like the Son of Man was coming among the clouds of heaven; who came forward to the Ancient of many days and presented him before Him. And he gave him power, honor and the kingdom: And all peoples, tribes and languages ​​will serve him: his power is eternal power, which will not be taken away from him, and his kingdom is indestructible[10]. Did not the holy evangelists see those words of Zechariah where he predicts the meek King who, climbing on a donkey and her colt, would enter Jerusalem, as Righteous and as Savior, amidst the acclamations of the crowds[11], were they not realized and confirmed?

9. On the other hand, this same doctrine about Christ the King that we have culled from the books of the Old Testament is so far from lacking in those of the New that, on the contrary, it is magnificently and luminously confirmed.

10. From this doctrine common to the Sacred Books, it necessarily followed that the Church, the kingdom of Christ on earth, destined to extend to all men and all nations, celebrated and glorified with multiplied displays of veneration, during the annual cycle of the liturgy, its Author and Founder as the Sovereign Lord and King of kings.

11. To show now what the foundation of this dignity and this power of Jesus Christ consists of, here is what Saint Cyril of Alexandria writes very well: Christ possesses sovereignty over all creatures, not torn by force nor taken from anyone, but by virtue of his own essence and nature[20]. That is to say, the sovereignty or principality of Christ is founded on the wonderful union called hypostatic. From which it follows that Christ must not only be worshiped as God by angels and by men, but, in addition, both are subject to his empire and must also obey him as man; so that by the mere fact of the hypostatic union, Christ has power over all creatures.

12. But, furthermore, what can be sweeter and gentler for us than the thought that Christ rules over us, not only by right of nature, but also by right of conquest, acquired at the cost of redemption? I wish that all men, very forgetful, would remember how much we have cost our Savior. You were redeemed not with gold or silver, which are perishable things, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of an Immaculate and blameless Lamb[21]. We are no longer ours, since Christ has bought us with a great price[22]; Even our very bodies are members of Jesus Christ[23].

13. Coming now to explain the strength and nature of this principality and sovereignty of Jesus Christ, we will briefly indicate that it contains a triple power, without which a true and proper principality is barely conceivable. The testimonies, adduced from the Holy Scriptures, regarding the universal empire of our Redeemer, prove more than sufficiently what we have said; and it is also a dogma of the Catholic faith that Jesus Christ was given to men as Redeemer, in whom they must trust, and as legislator whom they must obey[24]. The holy Gospels not only narrate that Christ legislated, but they present him to us legislating. In different circumstances and with different expressions the Divine Master says that those who keep his precepts will demonstrate that they love him and will remain in his charity[25]. Jesus himself, when responding to the Jews, who accused him of having violated the Sabbath with the wonderful healing of the paralytic, affirms that the Father had given him judicial power, because the Father does not judge anyone, but gave all the power to judge to the Son[26]. In which is also understood his right to reward and punish men, even during their mortal life, because this cannot be separated from a form of judgment. Furthermore, the so-called executive power must be attributed to Jesus Christ, since it is necessary that everyone obey his command, a power that inflicts punishments on rebels, from which no one can escape.

14. However, the texts that we have cited from Scripture demonstrate very evidently, and Jesus Christ himself confirms it with his way of acting, that this kingdom is primarily spiritual and refers to spiritual things. Indeed, on several occasions, when the Jews, and even the apostles themselves, mistakenly imagined that the Messiah would restore freedom to the people and reestablish the kingdom of Israel, Christ took away and tore away this vain imagination and hope. Likewise, when he was going to be proclaimed King by the crowd, which, full of admiration, surrounded him, He refused such title of honor by fleeing and hiding in solitude. Finally, in the presence of the Roman governor he stated that his kingdom was not of this world. This kingdom is shown to us in the gospels with such characters that men, to enter it, must prepare themselves by doing penance and cannot enter except by faith and baptism, which, although it is an external rite, means and produces internal regeneration. This kingdom is only opposed to the kingdom of Satan and the power of darkness; and he demands of his subjects not only that, their souls being detached from earthly things and riches, they keep orderly customs and hunger and thirst for justice, but also that they deny themselves and take up their cross. Having Christ, as Redeemer, rescued the Church with his Blood and offering himself, as Priest and as Victim, for the sins of the world, an offering that is perpetually renewed every day, who does not see that the royal dignity of the Savior is clothed and participates in the spiritual nature of both offices?

15. On the other hand, it would be seriously wrong to deny to Christ-Man the power over all human and temporal things, since the Father conferred upon him a most absolute right over created things, in such a way that all are subject to his discretion. Notwithstanding this, while he lived on earth he entirely abstained from exercising this power, and just as he then despised the possession and care of human things, so he also permitted, and continues to permit, their possessors to use them.

16. He is, in effect, the source of public and private good. Outside of Him we do not have to look for salvation in anyone else; For no other name under heaven has been given to men by which we must be saved.[29]

17. On the other hand, if men, publicly and privately, recognize the royal power of Christ, incredible benefits will necessarily come to all civil society, such as just freedom, tranquility and discipline, peace and concord. The royal dignity of Our Lord, just as it makes sacred in a certain way the human authority of the heads and rulers of the State, so it also ennobles the duties and obedience of the subjects. That is why the apostle Saint Paul, although he ordered married women and servants to reverence Christ in the person of their husbands and masters, also warned them not to obey them as simple men, but only as representatives of Christ, because it is unworthy of men redeemed by Christ to serve other men: You have been rescued at great cost; do not want to become servants of men[32].

18. And if the legitimately elected princes and rulers are persuaded that they rule, more than by right by command and on behalf of the divine King, it will not be hidden from anyone how holy and wisely they will have to use their authority and how great an account they will have, in giving the laws and demanding their compliance, with the common good and with the human dignity of their inferiors. From this will undoubtedly follow the stable flowering of tranquility and order, suppressing all causes of sedition; For although the citizen sees in the ruler or other public authorities men of a nature equal to his own and even unworthy and blameworthy for anything, he will not refuse to obey them when he contemplates in them the image and authority of Jesus Christ, God and true man.

19. As far as concord and peace are concerned, it is evident that the vaster the kingdom is and the greater the extent to which it embraces the human race, the more the bond of brotherhood that unites them takes root in the conscience of men. This conviction, just as it distances and dissipates frequent conflicts, also sweetens and reduces their bitterness. And if the kingdom of Christ embraced all men in fact, as it embraces them by right, why should we not expect that peace which the peaceful King brought to the earth, that King who came to reconcile all things; that he did not come to be served, but to serve; that being the Lord of all, he made himself an example of humility and established this virtue as the main law, united with the mandate of charity; who finally said: My yoke is easy and my burden is light.

20. Now, in order for these priceless benefits to be reaped more abundantly and to live stably in Christian society, it is necessary that the knowledge of the royal dignity of our Savior be spread as widely as possible, for which nothing will be more effective than instituting the proper and peculiar festival of Christ the King.

21. On the other hand, historical documents demonstrate that these festivities were instituted one after another in the course of the centuries, as the needs and usefulness of the Christian people demanded, that is, when it was necessary to strengthen them against a common danger, or defend them against the insidious errors of heresy, or encourage them and enkindle them more frequently so that they would know and venerate with greater devotion some mystery of the faith, or some benefit of divine goodness. Thus, from the first centuries of Christianity, when the faithful were bitterly persecuted, the liturgy began to commemorate the martyrs so that, as Saint Augustine says, the festivities of the martyrs were so many exhortations to martyrdom[34]. Later, the liturgical honors granted to holy confessors, virgins and widows served wonderfully to rekindle in the faithful the love of virtues, so necessary even in peaceful times. Above all, the festivities instituted in honor of the Blessed Virgin contributed, without a doubt, to the Christian people not only fervorizing their worship of the Mother of God, their most powerful protector, but also to burning them with a stronger love for the Heavenly Mother that the Redeemer had bequeathed them as an inheritance. Furthermore, among the benefits produced by the public and legitimate worship of the Virgin and the Saints, the fact that the Church has at all times been able to victoriously reject the plague of errors and heresies should not be passed over in silence.

22. At this point we must admire the designs of divine Providence, which, just as it usually brings good out of evil, so it also sometimes allowed the faith and piety of the faithful to cool, or for false doctrines to threaten Catholic truth, although in the end it returned to shine with new brilliance, and the faithful returned, awakened from their lethargy, to become fervent in virtue and holiness. Likewise, the festivities included in the liturgical year during modern times have also had the same origin and have produced identical fruits. Thus, when the reverence and worship of the Blessed Sacrament weakened, the feast of Corpus Christi was instituted, and it was ordered to be celebrated in such a way that the liturgical solemnity and magnificence lasted throughout the octave, to attract the faithful to publicly venerate the Lord. Likewise, the festival of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus was instituted when the souls, weakened and depressed by the sad and icy severity of the Jansenists, had grown cold and distanced themselves from the love of God and the confidence of their eternal salvation.

23. And if we now command that Christ the King be honored by all the Catholics of the world, with this we will also provide for the needs of the present times, and we will provide a very effective remedy to the plague that infects human society today. We consider the so-called secularism with its errors and abominable attempts to be the pest of our times; and you know, venerable brothers, that such impiety did not mature in a single day, but rather had been incubating long before in the bowels of society. It began by denying the empire of Christ over all people; The Church was denied the right, founded on the right of Christ himself, to teach the human race, that is, to give laws and direct people to lead them to eternal happiness. Then, little by little, the Christian religion was equated with the other false religions and unseemly lowered to their level. It was then subjected to civil power and the arbitrary permission of rulers and magistrates. And further progress was made: there were some of these who imagined replacing the religion of Christ with a certain natural religion, with certain purely human feelings. There was no shortage of States that believed they could do without God, and placed their religion on impiety and contempt for God.

24. The very bitter fruits that this distancing from Christ on the part of individuals and nations has produced so frequently and for so long, we have already lamented in our encyclical Ubi arcano, and we lament them again today, seeing the germ of discord sown everywhere; the hatred and rivalries that still delay the reestablishment of peace so much are kindled among the people; unbridled greed, which is often hidden under the appearance of public good and patriotic love; and, arising from all this, civil discord, together with a blind and unleashed selfishness, only attentive to its particular benefits and comforts and measuring everything by them; domestic peace destroyed at its roots by the forgetfulness and relaxation of family duties; it breaks the union and stability of families; and, finally, human society was shaken and pushed to death.

25. We are encouraged, however, by the sweet hope that the annual feast of Christ the King, which will soon be celebrated, will happily prompt society to turn to our most beloved Savior. Preparing and accelerating this return with action and work would certainly be the duty of Catholics; But many of them seem to have neither the position nor the authority in so-called social coexistence, which is unworthy of those who carry the torch of truth before them. These disadvantages perhaps come from the apathy and timidity of the good, who refrain from fighting or resist weakly; Therefore it is necessary that the adversaries of the Church gain greater recklessness and audacity. But if the faithful all understand that they must fight with tireless effort under the banner of Christ the King, then, inflamed by the fire of the apostolate, they will dedicate themselves to bringing the rebellious and ignorant to God again, and they will work courageously to keep the rights of the Lord intact.

26. And who does not notice that since the end of the last century the way to the institution of this festival was being wonderfully prepared? No one ignores how wisely and eloquently this cult was defended in numerous books published in a great variety of languages ​​and all over the world; and also that the empire and sovereignty of Christ was recognized with the pious practice of dedicating and consecrating almost countless families to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus. And not only families were consecrated, but also cities and nations. Furthermore: by the initiative and desire of Leo XIII, the entire human race was consecrated to the Divine Heart during the Holy Year of 1900.

27. It should not be ignored that, to solemnly confirm this sovereignty of Christ over human society, the very frequent Eucharistic Congresses that are usually celebrated in our times served in a wonderful way, and whose purpose is to summon the faithful of each of the dioceses, regions, nations and even the entire world, to venerate and adore Christ the King, hidden under the Eucharistic veils; and through speeches in the assemblies and in the temples, the adoration, in common, of the august Sacrament publicly exposed and of very solemn processions, to proclaim Christ as King who has been given to us by heaven. It could well and rightly be said that the Christian people, moved as if by divine inspiration, bringing out of the silence and hiding place of the temples that same Jesus whom the wicked, when he came into the world, did not want to receive, and leading him as a victor through the public roads, want to restore him in all his royal rights.

28. Now, to realize our idea that we have just explained, the Holy Year, which is coming to an end, offers us such an opportunity that there will be no better one; since God, having most benignly raised the minds and hearts of the faithful to the consideration of heavenly goods that surpass sense, has returned to them the gift of his grace, or has confirmed them on the right path, giving them new stimuli to emulate better charisms. Now, then, let us heed as many supplications as have been made, now let us consider the events of the Holy Year, in truth there are plenty of reasons to convince us that the day, so vehemently desired, has finally arrived when we announce that Christ as King of the entire human race must be honored with his own and special celebration.

29. Because in this year, as we said at the beginning, the divine King, truly admirable in his saints, has been gloriously magnified with the elevation of a new group of his faithful soldiers to the honor of the altars. Likewise, this year, through an unusual Mission Exhibition, everyone has been able to admire the triumphs that his evangelical workers have won for Christ by extending his kingdom. Finally, this year, with the celebration of the centenary of the Council of Nicaea, we have commemorated the vindication of the dogma of the consubstantiality of the incarnate Word with the Father, on which the sovereignty of Christ himself over all peoples rests as its own foundation.

30. Therefore, with our apostolic authority, we establish the feast of our Lord Jesus Christ the King, and decree that it be celebrated in all parts of the earth on the last Sunday of October, that is, the Sunday immediately preceding the feast of All Saints. We also order that on that day the consecration of the entire human race to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus be renewed every year, with the same formula that our predecessor of holy memory, Pius X, ordered to be recited annually.

31. It is not necessary, venerable brothers, that we explain to you in detail the reasons why we have decreed that the festival of Christ the King be celebrated separately from those others in which this same royal dignity seems already indicated and implicitly solemnized. It is enough to note that, although in all the festivals of our Lord the material object of them is Christ, their formal object is entirely different from the title and royal power of Jesus Christ. The reason why we wanted to establish this festivity on a Sunday is so that not only the clergy honor Christ the King with the celebration of the mass and the recitation of the divine office, but also so that the people, free from worries and with a spirit of holy joy, give Christ a clear testimony of their obedience and devotion. We also found the last Sunday of October much more suitable for this festival than all the others, because the liturgical year almost ends there; For thus it will come to pass that the mysteries of the life of Christ, commemorated in the course of the year, will end and receive crowning in this solemnity of Christ the King, and before celebrating the glory of All Saints, the glory of him who triumphs in all the saints and elect will be celebrated and exalted. Therefore, be it your duty and your office, venerable brothers, to ensure that the celebration of this annual festival is preceded, on certain days, by a course of preaching to the people in all the parishes, so that, with the faithful carefully instructed about the nature, significance and importance of this festival, they undertake and order a type of life that is truly worthy of those who long to lovingly and faithfully serve their King, Jesus Christ.

32. Before finishing this letter, it pleases us, venerable brothers, to briefly indicate the benefits that for the good, both of the Church and of civil society, and of each of the faithful, we expect and promise ourselves from this public homage of worship to Christ the King.

33. The celebration of this festival, which will be renewed every year, will also teach the nations that the duty to publicly worship and obey Jesus Christ is not only binding on individuals, but also on magistrates and rulers.

34. For if all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ our Lord; if men, because they have been redeemed by his blood, are subject by a new title to his authority; If, in short, this power embraces all human nature, it is clearly seen that there is no faculty in us that escapes such high sovereignty. It is, therefore, necessary that Christ reign in the intelligence of man, which, with perfect compliance, must firmly and constantly assent to the revealed truths and the doctrine of Christ; It is necessary that it reign in the will, which must obey the divine laws and precepts; It is necessary that it reign in the heart, which, postponing natural effects, must love God above all things, and be united only to Him; It is necessary that it reign in the body and in its members, which as instruments, or in the phrase of the apostle Saint Paul, as weapons of justice for God[35], must serve for the internal sanctification of the soul. All of which, if proposed to the meditation and deep consideration of the faithful, there is no doubt that they will more easily incline to perfection.

35. May the Lord, venerable brothers, grant that all who are outside his kingdom desire and receive the gentle yoke of Christ; May all of us who, through His mercy, are already His subjects and children, bear this yoke not reluctantly, but with pleasure, with love and holiness, and may our lives, always conformed to the laws of the divine kingdom, be rich in beautiful and abundant fruits; so that, being considered by Christ as good and faithful servants, we may become with Him participants in the heavenly kingdom, in its eternal happiness and glory.
